note: Some tablets can be bought from a pharmacy for period pain, by adults and teenagers aged 15 and over
evidence: NHS 'Who can and cannot take naproxen' (as summarised by the search tool): adults and teenagers aged 15 and over can buy naproxen from a pharmacy for period pain. An emc result for Boots Period Pain Reliever 250 mg (naproxen) describes that pharmacy product as for period pain in women aged 15 to 50, so the licensed upper age of 50 is not in the note or in the NHS wording (minor, not an error). dm+d lists the Feminax Ultra brand as discontinued; the note names no brand, which is right.

note: Most forms and uses of naproxen need a prescription
evidence: NHS naproxen pages (as summarised): naproxen is prescribed for arthritis, gout, period pain and muscle or bone problems, and you can buy some types from pharmacies but others are only available with a prescription. Only the period-pain tablets are described as pharmacy supply, so 'most forms and uses' is a fair reading. The word 'most' is the checker's inference, not an NHS phrase.

note: Nexium Control tablets for short-term heartburn in adults have been on general sale since 2015, in small packs
evidence: GOV.UK/MHRA news item 'Nexium Control 20mg Tablets now available for general sale' and the public assessment report 'Reclassification of Nexium Control 20mg Gastro-Resistant Tablets' (dated 27 January 2015, after a consultation in July 2014): pharmacy to general sale list, adults, reflux symptoms such as heartburn, maximum pack 14 tablets, no more than 2 weeks without seeing a doctor. emc still lists 'Nexium Control 20 mg gastro-resistant tablets (GSL)' (product 3660). NHS About esomeprazole says the lowest-strength tablets and capsules can be bought from pharmacies or shops. Answer to the 20 mg question: both classes exist now - GSL packs (max 14 tablets) and a separate emc listing 'Nexium Control 20 mg gastro-resistant tablets (P)' with 7, 14 and 28 tablet packs.

note: Some lowest-strength tablets are sold from pharmacies without a prescription
evidence: NHS About esomeprazole (as summarised): available on prescription, or you can buy the lowest-strength tablets and capsules from pharmacies or shops. emc also lists a separate 'Nexium Control 20 mg gastro-resistant tablets (P)' product (packs of 7, 14 and 28 tablets) alongside the GSL listing, so a pharmacy-only version exists as well as the general-sale one.

note: Higher strengths and other uses need a prescription
evidence: NHS About esomeprazole (as summarised): esomeprazole is available on prescription, and only the lowest-strength tablets and capsules are sold without one. The non-prescription Nexium Control licence is limited to adults aged 18 and over, 20 mg a day, up to 14 tablets and up to 2 weeks without consulting a doctor (MHRA public assessment report), so higher strengths and other uses need a prescription. This is implied rather than stated word for word.

note: Tablets for people aged 12 and over are sold in pharmacies and supermarkets
evidence: NHS About fexofenadine (as summarised): you can buy 120 mg fexofenadine tablets for adults and children aged 12 and over from pharmacies and supermarkets; 180 mg tablets (for hives) from pharmacies; tablets for children under 12 are on prescription only. emc SmPC (Telfast 120 mg): 120 mg once daily for adults and children aged 12 and over, not studied in under 12s. Caveats: the emc listings retrieved did not show a legal category (one fexofenadine leaflet in the results is POM), so the general-sale status rests on the NHS 'supermarkets' wording. The 180 mg tablets are pharmacy-only, so '120 mg tablets' would be more exact than 'Tablets' (optional tightening).

note: A small pack of tablets can be bought from a pharmacy by people who have already been diagnosed with migraine
evidence: NHS About sumatriptan (as summarised): you can buy packs containing two 50 mg tablets from a pharmacy without a prescription, but only if you have previously been diagnosed with migraine - so a prior diagnosis IS required. dm+d lists the branded Imigran Recovery 2-tablet pack as discontinued (28 Nov 2018) but the current NHS page still describes the pharmacy supply; the note names no brand so it is unaffected. Age limits for the pharmacy pack (the Imigran licence is 18 to 65) were not retrieved from a pharmacy-product page, so none is added.

note: Other tablet packs, the nasal spray and the injection need a prescription
evidence: NHS About sumatriptan (as summarised): it comes as tablets, nasal spray and injection and is available on prescription; the only non-prescription supply described is the pack of two 50 mg tablets for people already diagnosed with migraine, so other tablet packs, the nasal spray and the injection need a prescription (implied).

note: People aged 12 and over can buy it from pharmacies and shops for short-term diarrhoea
evidence: NHS loperamide pages (as summarised): you can buy loperamide from pharmacies and shops; children aged 12 and over can buy it for short-term diarrhoea, with the same dose as adults; shop-bought supply is limited to 6 capsules or tablets in 24 hours and not more than 48 hours without talking to a doctor.

note: Children aged 11 and under, and adults with long-lasting diarrhoea, need a prescription
evidence: NHS loperamide pages (as summarised): do not give loperamide to children under 12 unless a doctor prescribes it (the same as aged 11 and under); it is also available on prescription for some bowel conditions; children aged 12 to 17 with IBS or long-lasting diarrhoea take it on prescription only; shop-bought supply is for short-term use. The adult 'long-lasting diarrhoea' half follows from the same limits but was not quoted for adults in the retrieved text.

note: Adults can buy it from a pharmacy for constipation
evidence: NHS lactulose pages (as summarised): lactulose is available on prescription and to buy from pharmacies. An NHS integrated care board self-care guide (NHS Somerset) describes Lactulose solution (Duphalac) as a P (pharmacy-only) medicine.

note: Children under 14 need a prescription
evidence: NHS 'Who can and cannot take lactulose' (as summarised): children under 14 should not be given lactulose unless their doctor says it is OK, so pharmacy purchase is not for under-14s. The NHS Somerset self-care guide lists 'child under 14 years old' among the reasons a pharmacy cannot sell lactulose without a prescription. The age of 14 is therefore confirmed by two NHS sources. NHS wording is nearer 'only on a doctor's advice' than 'needs a prescription', but the practical effect is the same.

note: One lower-strength brand (Viagra Connect) is sold by pharmacists to men with erectile dysfunction after a consultation
evidence: The Viagra Connect part is supported: GOV.UK 'MHRA reclassifies Viagra Connect tablets to a Pharmacy medicine' - 50 mg, men over 18 with erectile dysfunction, one tablet a day, packs of up to 8, sold from pharmacies following a discussion with the pharmacist. The 'One ... brand' limit is NOT supported and is probably out of date: the NHS page says only that you can buy sildenafil from most pharmacies; emc and dm+d list other single-strength 50 mg sildenafil products for adult men with erectile dysfunction (Boots Sildenafil 50 mg, dm+d entry with start date 27-04-2026 and a 4-tablet pack; Durex Sildenafil 50mg; Liberize 50 mg; Aronix 50 mg); and a Kent and Medway formulary lists sildenafil 50 mg as over the counter. The legal category of those other products could not be read from the retrieved text, so I cannot prove a second pharmacy brand, but nothing retrieved says Viagra Connect is the only one.
suggestedNote: 50 mg sildenafil tablets (such as Viagra Connect) are sold by pharmacists to men aged 18 and over with erectile dysfunction after a consultation

note: One brand (Cialis Together) is sold by pharmacists to men with erectile dysfunction after a consultation
evidence: Core fact supported: GOV.UK 'MHRA reclassifies Cialis Together tablets to a Pharmacy medicine' - Cialis Together (tadalafil 10 mg) is available from pharmacies without a prescription for adult men with erectile dysfunction; it was the first tadalafil product made a pharmacy medicine. NHS Medicines Resources hosts a pharmacy guide, patient checklist and pharmacist quick guide for it, consistent with a pharmacist-led consultation (implied, not quoted). NOT established: that it is the only pharmacy tadalafil brand now. 'First' does not mean 'only', and sildenafil has gained several other 50 mg consumer brands since its own first reclassification. I did not run a tadalafil-generics search (budget used), so re-check before keeping 'One brand'.
suggestedNote: Cialis Together (tadalafil 10 mg) is sold by pharmacists to adult men with erectile dysfunction after a consultation

note: Other brands and strengths need a prescription
evidence: Partly supportable: the MHRA reclassification covers a 50 mg tablet only (one a day, packs of up to 8) and says medicines containing sildenafil remain available on prescription, so other strengths (emc lists 25, 50 and 100 mg sildenafil leaflets) and larger packs need a prescription. 'Other brands' is not supported and is probably wrong, because other single-strength 50 mg sildenafil brands are listed on emc and dm+d (Boots, Durex, Liberize, Aronix) and the NHS says sildenafil can be bought from most pharmacies; their legal category could not be read.
suggestedNote: Other strengths and larger packs need a prescription

note: Other brands and strengths need a prescription
evidence: Only the Cialis Together 10 mg product was reclassified to pharmacy (MHRA), which implies other tadalafil strengths stay prescription-only. No retrieved page states the legal class of other tadalafil brands, and the 'other brands' limb depends on Cialis Together being the only pharmacy brand, which is not established (see the tadalafil pharmacy note). The NHS tadalafil page was not retrieved within the search budget.

note: Cold sore cream can be bought from most pharmacies and shops
evidence: NHS About aciclovir (as summarised): aciclovir is available on prescription; you can buy aciclovir cold sore cream at most pharmacies and shops without a prescription.

note: Tablets and other forms mostly need a prescription
evidence: NHS About aciclovir (as summarised): tablets are generally prescription-only, and most types are only available with a prescription.

note: Capsules for vaginal thrush or balanitis can be bought from a pharmacy
evidence: NHS About fluconazole (as summarised): fluconazole is available on prescription; you can also buy it from a pharmacy for vaginal thrush or balanitis (brands include Azocan and Canesten Thrush Oral Capsules). The note gives no age limit; none was confirmed from the licence wording in the retrieved text (local NHS pharmacy protocols exclude under-16s and over-60s), so none is added.

note: Needed for other infections, longer courses and prevention
evidence: NHS About fluconazole (as summarised): other infections, including those in the blood or elsewhere in the body, need a prescription; thrush that keeps coming back follows a different schedule; pharmacy supply is limited to vaginal thrush or balanitis (single 150 mg dose). Longer courses and prevention are not named in the retrieved text but fall outside the pharmacy supply, so they follow by implication.
